title: Numbers & Math
summary: JavaScript stores all ordinary numbers in a single **number** type using 64-bit floating point, which is why integers and decimals share one type, why 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3, and why the Math object, parsing functions, and BigInt exist to help you work with numbers precisely.

subtopics.title: The number type (IEEE 754 doubles)
subtopics.explanation: JavaScript has one number type for everyday math, stored as a 64-bit IEEE 754 double-precision float. There is no separate int type, so 5 and 5.0 are the same value. This single type is convenient but means even whole numbers are held in floating-point form, which has limits on size and precision.

subtopics.title: Integers vs floats
subtopics.explanation: Although there is one type, you can treat numbers as integers or decimals. Integers are exact only up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 - 1); beyond that, precision is lost. Floats (decimals) can lose precision much sooner because many decimals cannot be represented exactly in binary.
subtopics.example:
console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER); // 9007199254740991
console.log(9007199254740991 + 2);    // 9007199254740992 (off by one)
console.log(Number.isInteger(5.0));   // true

subtopics.title: Floating-point precision (0.1 + 0.2)
subtopics.explanation: Because numbers are binary floats, fractions like 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be stored exactly, so their sum is slightly off. This is not a JavaScript bug — it is how IEEE 754 works in every language. Never compare floats with strict equality for money or fractions; compare within a small tolerance or work in integers.

subtopics.title: The Math object
subtopics.explanation: Math is a built-in object of math utilities and constants — you call its methods directly, never with new. Common ones include Math.round/floor/ceil for rounding, Math.max/min, Math.abs, Math.pow and Math.sqrt, and Math.random for a pseudo-random number in [0, 1). It also holds constants like Math.PI.

subtopics.title: Parsing & converting: parseInt, parseFloat, Number
subtopics.explanation: To turn strings into numbers you can use Number() (strict — the whole string must be numeric), parseInt() (reads leading integer digits, accepts a radix), or parseFloat() (reads a leading decimal). parseInt('12px') gives 12, while Number('12px') gives NaN. Always pass the radix to parseInt to avoid surprises.

subtopics.title: NaN and Infinity
subtopics.explanation: NaN ('Not a Number') is the result of invalid math like 0/0 or Number('abc'), and it is the only value not equal to itself, so use Number.isNaN to test for it. Infinity and -Infinity result from overflow or dividing by zero. Both are still of type 'number'.
subtopics.example:
console.log(0 / 0);              // NaN
console.log(NaN === NaN);        // false
console.log(Number.isNaN(NaN)); // true
console.log(1 / 0);             // Infinity

subtopics.title: toFixed and formatting
subtopics.explanation: toFixed(n) rounds a number to n decimal places and returns a string, which is handy for displaying money or percentages. Because it returns a string, convert back with Number() if you need to keep computing. For locale-aware formatting (commas, currency), use Intl.NumberFormat.

subtopics.title: BigInt intro
subtopics.explanation: When you need integers larger than Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (e.g., huge IDs, timestamps in nanoseconds), use BigInt, written with an n suffix or BigInt(). BigInts are exact for integers of arbitrary size but cannot be freely mixed with regular numbers in arithmetic, and they do not support decimals.

foundations.overview: JavaScript represents ordinary numbers with one type, the 64-bit IEEE 754 double. That design unifies integers and decimals but introduces floating-point rounding (0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3) and a safe-integer ceiling. The Math object, the parsing functions (Number, parseInt, parseFloat), special values (NaN, Infinity), toFixed, and BigInt are the tools you use to compute and display numbers reliably.
foundations.formalDefinition: The JavaScript number type is a primitive that stores values as IEEE 754 double-precision (64-bit) binary floating-point, giving about 15-17 significant decimal digits and exact integers only up to 2^53 - 1.
foundations.whyItMatters: Numbers drive prices, quantities, scores, timers, coordinates, and analytics. Misunderstanding floating-point precision or parsing leads to wrong totals, broken comparisons, and rounding bugs that users and businesses notice immediately.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of each number as a value squeezed into a fixed-width binary container. Whole numbers fit perfectly until they get very large, but many decimals can only be approximated — like trying to write 1/3 in a finite number of decimal digits. The tiny leftover error is what shows up in 0.1 + 0.2.
foundations.browserPerspective: Engines like V8 optimize integers that fit in a small range ('Smi') for speed and fall back to full doubles for larger or fractional values. This is invisible to you, but it is why integer-heavy code can be faster than float-heavy code.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Calculating cart totals (often in integer cents to avoid float errors), rounding prices with toFixed, generating random ids or dice rolls with Math.random, parsing user-typed numbers from inputs, and handling large database ids with BigInt.
foundations.businessImpact: Money math done in floats can produce off-by-a-cent totals that erode trust and fail audits; handling precision correctly protects revenue accuracy and compliance.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing the safe-integer limit, the right parser, and how to compare floats prevents a whole category of silent bugs in calculations and conditionals.
foundations.performanceImpact: Integer operations within the safe range are fast and exact; BigInt is slower than regular numbers, so reserve it for cases that genuinely exceed the safe-integer limit.
commonUseCases: Computing totals and applying rounding for display
Parsing numeric input from strings and form fields
Generating random values for ids, sampling, or games
Handling very large integers (ids, nanosecond timestamps) with BigInt

commonMisconceptions.myth: 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 is true, and if not it's a JavaScript bug.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's false because IEEE 754 binary floats cannot represent 0.1 and 0.2 exactly; this happens in nearly every language, so compare within a tolerance or use integer cents.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can check for NaN with x === NaN.
commonMisconceptions.reality: NaN is never equal to itself, so x === NaN is always false; use Number.isNaN(x) instead.

visualExplorer.caption: Trace how binary floating point introduces a tiny rounding error.

config.intro: Follow the addition 0.1 + 0.2 as the engine stores and adds these values in binary.

steps.name: Store 0.1
steps.detail: 0.1 has no exact binary representation, so it is stored as the nearest 64-bit float (slightly above 0.1).

steps.name: Store 0.2
steps.detail: 0.2 also cannot be represented exactly and is stored as the nearest float (slightly above 0.2).

steps.name: Add the approximations
steps.detail: The two slightly-off values are added, and the small errors combine.

steps.name: Round the result
steps.detail: The sum is rounded to the nearest representable double, which is 0.30000000000000004.

steps.name: Compare to 0.3
steps.detail: 0.3 stored as a float differs from that sum, so 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 is false.

steps.name: Compare safely
steps.detail: Check Math.abs(sum - 0.3) < 1e-9 (a tolerance) instead of strict equality.

interactiveExamples.title: Floating-point in action
interactiveExamples.explanation: See the classic precision result and how to compare floats safely with a small tolerance (epsilon).

sandbox.code:
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);            // 0.30000000000000004
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);    // false

const nearlyEqual = Math.abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < 1e-9;
console.log('close enough?', nearlyEqual); // true

debuggingLab.title: The NaN comparison that never matches
debuggingLab.symptom: The guard never catches invalid input — 'invalid' is never logged even when the number is NaN.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: NaN is the only value in JavaScript that is not equal to itself, so value === NaN is always false even when value is NaN. The check can never succeed, so the invalid branch is unreachable.
commonMistakes: Assuming Number('abc') throws instead of returning NaN.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make the code correctly detect when value is NaN.

theory.question: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not equal 0.3 in JavaScript?
theory.directAnswer: Because JavaScript numbers are IEEE 754 binary floating-point, and 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation. They are stored as the nearest approximations, and adding them yields 0.30000000000000004, which differs from the stored value of 0.3, so the strict comparison is false.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A precision limitation of binary floating-point arithmetic, not a JavaScript-specific bug.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Just as 1/3 cannot be written exactly in finite decimals, 0.1 cannot be written exactly in finite binary, so it is rounded to fit 64 bits.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The approximations of 0.1 and 0.2 are summed and rounded to the nearest representable double, which is slightly more than 0.3.

theory.whyImportant: It affects money and measurement math; comparing floats with === or summing them naively produces wrong results unless handled.
theory.realWorldExample: Summing prices as floats can yield 0.30000000000000004 for a $0.30 total; storing amounts in integer cents avoids it.

nestedTopics.title: Epsilon comparison
nestedTopics.explanation: Compare with Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON or a small tolerance.

nestedTopics.title: Integer cents
nestedTopics.explanation: Do money math in whole cents and divide only for display.

followUps.question: How should you compare two floats for equality?
followUps.answer: Compare the absolute difference against a small tolerance (epsilon), e.g. Math.abs(a - b) < 1e-9, rather than using ===.

followUps.question: How do you avoid this for currency?
followUps.answer: Store and compute amounts in integer minor units (cents), then format to two decimals only when displaying.

theory.question: What is the difference between Number(), parseInt(), and parseFloat()?
theory.directAnswer: Number() converts the entire string and returns NaN if any part is non-numeric. parseInt() reads the leading integer (and takes a radix), stopping at the first invalid character. parseFloat() reads a leading decimal number. So '12px' becomes NaN with Number but 12 with parseInt.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Three ways to turn strings into numbers with different strictness and behavior.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Number is the strict, whole-string converter; parseInt/parseFloat exist to extract numbers from mixed strings like '12px' or '3.14em'.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: parseInt scans leading digits in the given radix; parseFloat scans a leading floating-point literal; Number coerces the full trimmed string or returns NaN.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the wrong one causes NaN where you expected a value, or a truncated value where you expected NaN.
theory.realWorldExample: Reading '16px' from a computed CSS style needs parseInt('16px', 10) to get 16; Number would give NaN.

nestedTopics.title: Radix argument
nestedTopics.explanation: Always pass 10 to parseInt to avoid octal/hex surprises.

nestedTopics.title: Unary plus
nestedTopics.explanation: +str is a terse equivalent of Number(str).

followUps.question: Why always pass the radix to parseInt?
followUps.answer: Without it, leading '0x' is treated as hexadecimal and behavior can vary; passing 10 forces decimal parsing and predictable results.

scenario.question: Your shopping cart shows totals like $0.30000000000000004 and occasionally a cent off. How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The cause is summing prices as floating-point numbers. I'd switch to integer-cent math: convert each price to cents with Math.round(price * 100), sum those integers exactly, then divide by 100 and toFixed(2) only for display. That removes the drift.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A floating-point accumulation error in money calculations.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Decimal prices are inexact in binary, so summing many of them compounds small errors.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Working in integer cents keeps every value exact within the safe-integer range; conversion to dollars happens once at the end.

scenario.whyImportant: Incorrect monetary totals damage trust and can fail accounting checks, making this a common practical interview scenario.

nestedTopics.title: Integer cents
nestedTopics.explanation: Represent money as whole minor units to stay exact.

nestedTopics.title: toFixed for display
nestedTopics.explanation: Format only at the boundary, keeping computation in integers.

followUps.question: When would you reach for a decimal/BigInt library instead?
followUps.answer: For currencies with more than two decimals, very large sums beyond safe integers, or strict financial rounding rules, a dedicated decimal library or BigInt-based amounts is safer.

coding.question: Write a function randomInt(min, max) that returns a random integer between min and max inclusive.
coding.thoughtProcess: Math.random() gives a float in [0, 1). I want an inclusive range of size (max - min + 1). I multiply random by that size, floor it to get an offset from 0 to size-1, then add min. Flooring keeps the upper bound inclusive because random never reaches 1.
coding.lineByLine: Math.random() returns a value in [0, 1). Multiplying by (max - min + 1) scales it to [0, range). Math.floor drops the fractional part to give an integer 0..range-1, and adding min shifts it into [min, max]. The +1 makes max reachable.

alternativeApproaches.title: Exclusive upper bound
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Drop the +1 to make max exclusive, matching array-index use cases.

followUps.question: Is Math.random suitable for security tokens?
followUps.answer: No — it is pseudo-random and predictable; use crypto.getRandomValues for security-sensitive randomness.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Numeric handling spans the UI (formatting, input parsing) and the data layer (totals, ids). Centralizing money math in integer-cent helpers and formatting in an Intl wrapper keeps numeric behavior consistent and testable.
productionDeepDive.performance: Integer arithmetic within the safe range is fast and exact; BigInt is significantly slower, so use it only when values exceed Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. Avoid unnecessary string conversions in hot numeric loops.
productionDeepDive.security: Use crypto.getRandomValues, not Math.random, for tokens or anything that must be unpredictable. Validate and clamp parsed numeric input to avoid overflow or out-of-range values driving logic.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Large integer ids from databases can exceed the safe-integer limit and silently lose precision when received as JSON numbers; transport them as strings or BigInt to preserve exactness.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Prefer named constants (Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, Number.EPSILON), explicit radixes in parseInt, and dedicated formatting helpers so numeric intent is clear and bugs are easy to spot.
productionDeepDive.observability: Log unexpected NaN or Infinity results with context; they often indicate bad parsing or division-by-zero upstream and are easy to miss because they propagate silently.

caseStudies.problem: Float-based money math produced off-by-a-cent totals and failed reconciliation.
caseStudies.solution: Moved all monetary values to integer minor units and formatted only for display.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: A conversion boundary to manage in exchange for exact totals.
caseStudies.lessons: Never represent money as floating-point; integer cents (or a decimal library) is the reliable pattern.

keyTakeaways: JavaScript has a single number type: 64-bit IEEE 754 doubles, so integers and decimals share one type with limited precision.
0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 because binary floats can't represent those decimals exactly — compare floats with a tolerance, not ===.
Use Number (strict), parseInt (leading integer, with a radix), or parseFloat (leading decimal) to convert strings to numbers.
NaN is never equal to itself (use Number.isNaN), Infinity comes from overflow/divide-by-zero, and both are of type 'number'.
toFixed rounds to a string for display; do money math in integer cents, and use BigInt only for integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER.
